clue.text: Fictional memoirist upset about award given twice

indicators.note: given twice tells us to write the assembled piece two times in a row
about places the hurt feeling around the honour

parts.note: upset as an adjective means hurt
the MBE is a British honour, Member of the Order of the British Empire

explanation.surface: A novelist's narrator is cross about receiving the same prize two times.
explanation.walkthrough: Nabokov's narrator of Lolita tells his story as a memoir written in prison; 'upset' is an adjective here, hurt, not a reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Nabokov's Lolita is framed as the confession of its narrator, an invented character writing his own life story.

clue.text: Extremely high peak for Saki

indicators.note: extremely means at the extremes, the first and last letters of the word high

parts.note: a Munro is a Scottish mountain over 3,000 feet

explanation.surface: A very lofty summit chosen for the short-story writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' takes H and H, the first and last letters of 'high'. Saki was the pen name of Hector Hugh Munro.
explanation.definitionFit: Saki was the pseudonym of the Edwardian short-story writer Hector Hugh Munro, so his initials and surname name the same author.

clue.text: Event in 1969 show behind Howards End location?

parts.note: to moon is to show one's bare behind
a landing is a spot in a house, such as the house at Howards End in E M Forster's novel

explanation.surface: A 1969 happening displayed after the setting of Forster's Howards End.
explanation.walkthrough: 'show behind' is a verb phrase: baring one's backside. Howards End is the house in Forster's novel; a landing is a place in a house, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Apollo 11 put astronauts on the lunar surface in July 1969, the most famous event of that year.

clue.text: What follows Oedipus, missing opening set of scenes, right?

indicators.note: missing opening means the first letter has been taken off

parts.note: Rex follows Oedipus in the title of Sophocles' play Oedipus Rex
an act is a division of a play made up of several scenes

explanation.surface: A theatre question: is it correct that the next part of Oedipus lacks its opening scenes?
explanation.walkthrough: Sophocles' play is known in English as Oedipus Rex, so 'What follows Oedipus' is its second title word.
explanation.definitionFit: Right in the sense of correct or precise matches a word meaning accurate.

clue.text: Author who wrote for children, mostly about crime

indicators.note: mostly means most of the name, the last letter left off

parts.note: Geoffrey Trease wrote historical novels for children
on means about, as in a book on a subject

explanation.surface: A children's writer whose stories are largely about wrongdoing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Author who wrote for children' looks like the definition, but the definition is 'crime' at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Treason, betraying one's country or sovereign, is a serious criminal offence.

clue.text: Stress beneath bit of verse

parts.note: beneath means under
a line is a single row of a poem

explanation.surface: Emphasis falls below a fragment of poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: To stress a point is to emphasise it, as drawing a rule under words does on the page.

clue.text: Austen heroine avoiding Anne after first venture

indicators.note: avoiding means keeping clear of, so the letters are removed from the surname

parts.note: Elizabeth Bennet is the heroine of Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice

indicators.note: after first means the name without its first letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Austen's heroine dodges Anne after an initial gamble.
explanation.walkthrough: Anne Elliot of Persuasion is another Austen heroine, which makes 'Anne' look like the definition; only its last three letters matter.
explanation.definitionFit: To venture money is to risk or wager it, as on a horse.

clue.text: Nobel laureate's problems leaving book trade

annotationWithheld.why: Nobel laureate's problems leaving book trade (7): RUSSELL fits the crossings and Bertrand Russell is a Nobel laureate, but no parse of 'problems leaving book trade' giving its letters has been found
annotationWithheld.clue: Nobel laureate's problems leaving book trade

clue.text: Mark initially misplaced, then recalled, content of magazine

indicators.note: recalled is read as called back, so the shortened punctuation word runs in reverse
initially misplaced says the first letter of the mark has gone missing

parts.note: a comma is a punctuation mark

explanation.surface: An editor loses a mark early on and then recalls what a magazine contains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially misplaced' drops the C of COMMA, leaving OMMA, and 'recalled' turns that round. The magazine is the cartridge chamber of a gun, not a periodical.
explanation.definitionFit: A gun's magazine holds cartridges, which is ammunition, shortened in slang.

clue.text: Sand to cite novel raconteur

indicators.note: novel as an adjective means new, so these letters take a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A request to quote George Sand, the French novelist, as a storyteller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book beside the writer George Sand, but it is the anagram signal for SAND TO CITE.
explanation.definitionFit: A raconteur is a skilled teller of stories, and one who trades in short amusing tales is a teller of anecdotes.

clue.text: Popular figures in Greek mythology holding large balloons

parts.note: popular means in, as in fashionable

indicators.note: holding says the popular figures wrap around the size letter

parts.note: the Fates are the three goddesses who spin and cut the thread of life
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Well-loved characters from Greek myth are shown carrying big balloons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'balloons' looks like a plural noun but is a verb: swells up.
explanation.definitionFit: To balloon is to swell or blow up, as prices or a tyre do when pumped with air.

clue.text: Character discontented when confused with Leah?

definitions.text: Character discontented when confused with Leah?

indicators.note: when confused signals a jumble of the letters gathered so far
discontented means with its contents emptied out, leaving only the outside letters of the word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A biblical figure is unhappy when mistaken for her sister Leah.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discontented' leaves C and R from Character; 'when confused' jumbles them with LEAH. In Genesis Laban swapped Leah for her younger sister at Jacob's wedding, so the two were famously confused.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis Jacob was tricked into marrying Leah in place of the younger sister he loved, so she was the woman confused with Leah.

clue.text: Antagonist of Julius Caesar suppressing response to stabbing, taking crown back for one idly watching

indicators.note: suppressing means holding down inside, so the senator's name surrounds the rest

parts.note: Cato the Younger was Caesar's bitter political opponent
ouch is what one cries when stabbed

indicators.note: back says the word for crown is read in reverse

parts.note: the crown is the top of the head

explanation.surface: Caesar's enemy stifles a cry at his assassination while picking up a crown again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking' is a link joining the cry to the reversed crown before both go inside Caesar's opponent.
explanation.definitionFit: A couch potato is an idle person who spends hours slumped in front of the television.

clue.text: Black Beauty etc in excellent site for Agenor tablets

parts.note: Black Beauty, Anna Sewell's horse, is one of many mounts, animals ridden
A1, written AI in crosswords, means first-rate

explanation.surface: Sewell's horse and others stand in a fine place where the setter keeps his tablets.
explanation.walkthrough: Agenor is this puzzle's setter, so 'Agenor tablets' are the setter's own tablets of stone; on Sinai Moses received the tablets of the law.
explanation.definitionFit: In Exodus the stone tablets bearing the Ten Commandments were given to Moses on this mountain.

clue.text: The Shell Seekers follow-up in a few weeks

definitions.meaning: Rosamunde Pilcher followed her bestseller The Shell Seekers with a novel named after the ninth month
the month that arrives a few weeks after late summer, when the puzzle appeared

explanation.definitionFit: Pilcher's sequel to The Shell Seekers is named after the ninth month, which also comes soon after August.

clue.text: Self-complacently disregarding shipwrecked men at first, like Caliban

indicators.note: disregarding means leaving out, so the selected letters are dropped from the adverb

parts.note: smugly means in a self-satisfied, self-complacent way

indicators.note: at first takes the opening letter of each of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone ignores the sailors cast ashore, as Shakespeare's monster in The Tempest might.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at first' gives S and M, which 'disregarding' removes from SMUGLY. Caliban in The Tempest is described as a deformed, misshapen creature.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare makes Caliban a misshapen monster, hideous to look at.

clue.text: Food writer shunning a shop

indicators.note: shunning means avoiding, so the word a is left out of the writer's name

parts.note: Delia Smith is a famous British cookery writer and TV cook

explanation.surface: A cookery writer refuses to set foot in a particular store.
explanation.walkthrough: DELIA, the first name of the British TV cook Delia Smith, loses A by 'shunning'.
explanation.definitionFit: A delicatessen is a small shop selling cooked meats, cheeses and prepared food.

clue.text: Appoint artist, a complex woman?

parts.note: to elect is to choose someone for an office, appoint
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: Choosing a painter, a complicated woman perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: Freud's pupil Jung named a complex after this Greek heroine, so she is a woman with a complex.
explanation.definitionFit: The Electra complex, named after the vengeful daughter of Agamemnon in Greek tragedy, is a psychological term.

clue.text: For the author, America is god

parts.note: pro means in favour of, for
the setter refers to himself as the author, so the word is me
taken as written
US is short for United States, America

explanation.surface: A writer claims that for him the United States is a deity.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are PRO, ME, then THE from 'the' and US; the Titan who stole fire for mankind.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titan who stole fire from Olympus is a divine being of Greek myth, so he counts as a deity.

clue.text: Eg Long John Silver struggling loads with lieutenant

indicators.note: struggling means wrestling about, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Stevenson's pirate staggers under heavy burdens alongside a junior officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is a link; the pirate of Treasure Island is the archetypal veteran seaman.
explanation.definitionFit: The pirate of Treasure Island is an experienced seaman, a veteran sailor of long service.

clue.text: Revised Edda put out

indicators.note: out means wrong or disordered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A new edition of the Norse Edda is published.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put out' reads as published, but 'out' is the anagram signal for EDDA PUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something revised has been brought up to date, corrected and amended.

clue.text: Hugo's article, fit for class

parts.note: Victor Hugo wrote in French, whose masculine definite article is le
an ague is a fit of shivering fever

explanation.surface: A piece of writing by Victor Hugo is suitable for a lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hugo's' points to French, as in Les Misérables; 'fit' is a noun, a bout of shaking, not an adjective meaning suitable.
explanation.definitionFit: A league is a grade or level of quality, as in saying someone is out of your class.

clue.text: Servant returned Bond's missing introduction, topic for Fleming in 1956

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the servant's word runs backwards

parts.note: a maid is a female servant

indicators.note: missing introduction means the opening letter has gone

parts.note: the possessive is read as the plural bonds

explanation.surface: A maid comes back without Bond, the spy at the heart of Ian Fleming's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns MAID to DIAM; 'missing introduction' takes B from BONDS. Fleming's 1956 novel was Diamonds Are Forever, and he wrote the non-fiction The Diamond Smugglers in 1957.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian Fleming's 1956 Bond novel centres on smuggled gems, as its title, Diamonds Are Forever, says.

clue.text: Review a Brian Cleeve novel without its jacket

indicators.note: without its jacket strips the book title of its outside letters, like a dust jacket removed

parts.note: Judith is a novel by the Irish writer Brian Cleeve

explanation.surface: A critic reviews a Brian Cleeve book after taking off its dust cover.
explanation.walkthrough: A book's jacket wraps its outside, so taking it off removes the outer letters of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: An audit is a formal examination or inspection, especially of accounts.

clue.text: Southern politician sounded fed up in sketches

parts.note: a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

indicators.note: sounded says the word for fed up is spoken, giving a word that sounds like it

parts.note: fed up means bored

explanation.surface: A Conservative from the south seemed weary in a set of drawings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sounded' turns BORED into BOARD, which sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A film storyboard is a sequence of drawings laying out the shots of a scene in order.

clue.text: Mock section of tragedy

indicators.note: section of means a part of the word, a run of its letters

explanation.surface: A scene that mocks a part of a tragic play.
explanation.definitionFit: To rag someone is to tease or make fun of them.

clue.text: Saviour of Frankenstein not using outside voice

indicators.note: not using outside means the first and last letters of the name are dropped

parts.note: in Mary Shelley's novel Captain Robert Walton rescues Victor Frankenstein from the Arctic ice

explanation.surface: Frankenstein's rescuer does not use a loud outdoor voice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not using outside' removes W and N from WALTON. 'outside voice' looks like a phrase about shouting, but it splits into indicator and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Alto is a singing voice, the lowest female range or a high male one.

clue.text: Dystopian in drama got to wear pants

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, poor stuff, so the letters are a mess to be rearranged

explanation.surface: In a play, an actor has to put on trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pants' looks like trousers to wear, but it is British slang for rubbish, the anagram signal for DRAMA GOT TO WEAR. The Canadian novelist wrote The Handmaid's Tale.
explanation.definitionFit: The Canadian novelist is known for The Handmaid's Tale, set in a repressive future, so she is a writer of grim imagined societies.
